title: NES Max / BPS-Max
subtitle: The first commercial sliding-disc game controller — a thumb-driven slide surface instead of a D-pad
why_scout_cares: The NES Max (1988), by Bullet-Proof Software (Henk Rogers), replaced the traditional D-pad with a sliding disc that glides in a recessed channel. The disc is a mechanical slide potentiometer action: sliding it registers directional input with a fluid, continuous feel that a conventional D-pad cannot produce. This is the museum's only sliding-mechanism game controller — a genuine early ancestor of the thumb-scroll and trackpad that would later appear on laptops and smartphones. Over 2 million units were sold. It is a strange, mass-market alternative to digital switches, and represents a physical input grammar entirely absent from the collection.

research.title: NES Max / BPS-Max (1988)
research.by: Bullet-Proof Software (Henk Rogers), licensed by Nintendo
research.overview: The NES Max is an officially licensed third-party controller for the Nintendo Entertainment System, manufactured by Bullet-Proof Software (Henk Rogers' company) and sold through Nintendo's distribution channels. Its defining feature is a sliding disc control pad that replaces the traditional D-pad. Rather than pivoting on a central post like a conventional cross-shaped D-pad, the Max's disc slides within a recessed channel, using mechanical contact registers to detect direction. This gives the user a thumb-driven slide surface — a continuous motion for directional input, rather than discrete switch closures. The controller also includes two programmable rapid-fire buttons (A and B). Over 2 million NES Max controllers were sold.

deepDive.heading: The sliding disc mechanism
deepDive.text: The NES Max disc sits in a circular recess and slides in any of the eight standard directions. Unlike a D-pad (which rocks on a pivot and closes membrane-switch contacts), the disc moves laterally within its housing, with the disc's position detected by sliding contacts that complete circuits for each direction. This gives a distinctly different feel: the thumb slides the disc rather than rocking it, providing a more continuous, smooth input action. In Japan, the version was called the BPS-Max (Bullet-Proof Software). Henk Rogers reported selling approximately 2 million units across both regions.

deepDive.heading: Place in controller evolution
deepDive.text: The NES Max predates by roughly a decade the thumb-driven slide surfaces that would become universal on laptops (TrackPoint-style pointing sticks, touchpads, and thumb-driven scroll discs). It represents an alternative path in game controller design — a path that replaced discrete mechanical contacts with a continuous slide surface. Though it did not directly spawn a lineage, thumb-driven analog surfaces would reappear on later controllers (Sony's DualShock analog sticks, Nintendo's Circle Pad), and the slide-disc concept specifically reappears in niche arcade controllers and the 'sliding pad' on certain handheld gaming devices.

deepDive.heading: Cultural significance
deepDive.text: The NES Max was heavily marketed as an 'advanced' controller with turbo-fire, and its distinctive sliding pad was its key selling point. It appears as one of the recognizable third-party NES peripherals, and its developer Henk Rogers is a significant figure in video game history (the publisher of Black Onyx, the first Japanese RPG, and later the Tetris rights holder). The controller demonstrates a willingness to experiment with physical input grammars even within the tightly constrained NES ecosystem.
